options.A: Prompts and answers get shorter, since 8-bit weights produce more compact tokens
options.B: The model needs fewer layers and a smaller vocabulary, so each decode tick has less work to do in total
options.C: Temperature can drop and sampling can be skipped, since 8-bit logits are already sharp
options.D: Each tick reads half the weight bytes, and the freed memory holds more KV caches for a bigger batch

options.A: Put a timestamp at the top so the cache can tell how old the prompt is and expire it in time
options.B: Fixed content first (system prompt, tools, examples); changing content (user message, time) last
options.C: User message first, so it gets the most attention, then the system prompt and tools after it
options.D: Order doesn't matter; the cache matches any shared stretch of text wherever it appears in the prompt

options.A: Total tokens per second rise a lot, each user's TPOT rises a little, and KV memory caps how many users fit
options.B: Both total throughput and each user's TPOT improve, since the GPU is busier and works more efficiently per token
options.C: Each user's TPOT stays exactly the same until compute runs out, and throughput rises 64 times
options.D: Total throughput stays the same, since the GPU is already busy; each user just gets 64 times slower

options.A: The number of tokens at which the chosen and rejected answers differ from each other
options.B: The reward model's score for the chosen answer minus its score for the rejected one, as in RLHF
options.C: The difference in length between the chosen and rejected answers, which DPO penalizes
options.D: How much more the model now favors chosen over rejected, compared with the starting model

options.A: Input cost: providers bill cached input tokens at a discount
options.B: TPOT: each output token gets much faster
options.C: TTFT: only the new tokens need prefill
options.D: The answer gets more accurate

options.A: RLHF: a reward model and reinforcement learning, generating during training. DPO: one loss on chosen/rejected pairs
options.B: Both need a trained reward model and sampled answers during training; DPO just trains its reward model faster
options.C: RLHF trains on single answers rated by people; DPO needs whole conversations, with every turn scored by people
options.D: RLHF: only human-written answers, trained like SFT. DPO: a reward model scoring the model's own answers

options.A: Rate limiting: each token may only attend to a fixed number of others per step
options.B: A dead-letter queue: future tokens are parked to one side and processed after the current one finishes
options.C: A load balancer: each token is routed only to the attention heads that are free
options.D: A snapshot read: each transaction sees only what committed before it, never later writes

options.A: SFT overwrites most of what pre-training learned, so a small set is enough to rebuild it
options.B: Pre-training is mostly wasted, since the useful skills only appear once SFT begins
options.C: SFT examples teach facts far more efficiently than pre-training tokens, so most knowledge comes from SFT
options.D: Knowledge comes from pre-training; a small, high-quality SFT set mainly shapes behavior and format

options.A: A bigger vocabulary
options.B: A higher busy share of each paid hour (traffic, autoscaling, sharing GPUs across models)
options.C: More tokens per second while busy (batching, quantization, better kernels)
options.D: Lower temperature

options.A: Nothing: training would crash, because softmax needs at least one masked score in every row
options.B: To generate whole sentences at once, since every position would see every other one at the same time
options.C: To copy the next token from the input, since it could see it; at generation that token doesn't exist yet
options.D: Exactly the same thing, only slower, since each position would also attend to positions it then ignores

options.A: Generation quietly retrains the model after each token so it stays in step with training
options.B: Both run at the same temperature, so the probabilities they compute come out identical
options.C: They don't match exactly; a short extra training phase adjusts the model so generation roughly agrees
options.D: The mask makes each position see only itself and earlier positions, exactly as during generation

options.A: A content-addressed cache with a TTL: hash prefix blocks, look them up, expire after minutes
options.B: A write-through cache in front of a database: every new prompt is written to the cache and to disk
options.C: A message queue: prompts wait until enough with the same prefix arrive to process them together
options.D: Database sharding: each prefix is pinned to one server, which keeps its cache forever

options.A: A smaller model labels the text first, and the large model then learns from those labels
options.B: Labels are added later during fine-tuning; pre-training only learns word statistics
options.C: It does need labels; they are crowdsourced, which is why pre-training costs so much
options.D: The text supplies the answer: the right label at each position is simply the next token

options.A: TTFT (time to first token): how long before anything appears
options.B: End-to-end latency: the time until the whole answer has finished
options.C: Throughput: total tokens per second across all users
options.D: Time to compute the KV cache size

options.A: Input tokens share each weight read in prefill; each output step reads all the weights to emit one token per user
options.B: Output tokens are longer than input tokens, because the model writes whole words rather than pieces
options.C: Output tokens pass through more layers than input tokens, since the model must also pick the next token
options.D: Providers charge more for output to discourage long answers; the GPU time per token is actually about the same

options.A: p − 1 for the correct token, and p for every other token
options.B: p for the correct token, and p − 1 for every other token
options.C: −ln p for the correct token, and 0 for every other token
options.D: 1 for the correct token, 0 for every other token

options.A: Set the attention weights above the diagonal to 0 after the weighted average has been taken
options.B: Add −∞ to scores above the diagonal before softmax, so future positions get exactly 0 weight
options.C: Multiply the values of future tokens by 0.5, so they count for half in the weighted average
options.D: Delete the future tokens from the input, so each position runs on a shorter sequence

options.A: Lowering the temperature: fewer candidate tokens per step, so each tick is faster
options.B: Adding GPUs (tensor parallelism): more bandwidth per tick and more room for caches
options.C: Quantizing to 8-bit: half the bytes per tick and room for twice the caches
options.D: Raising the batch size: more users share each weight read, so each user's TPOT drops

options.A: Prefill doesn't read the weights at all; it only builds the KV cache from the prompt's embeddings
options.B: Prefill results are already cached from earlier requests, so there is little left for it to speed up
options.C: Decode is memory-bound, so fewer weight bytes speed it up; prefill is compute-bound, so smaller weights barely help
options.D: Quantization only shrinks the output layer, which decode runs on every step but prefill runs only once per prompt

options.A: It isn't fully safe; small errors from a different request's context are accepted for the speed
options.B: The server re-checks every stored value against the new request and recomputes any that differ
options.C: Keys and values at position i depend only on tokens 1…i, so an identical prefix always gives identical KV
options.D: KV values come from the weights alone, so they are the same for every prompt and any stored copy works for any request

options.A: Return an error, since the prompt lacks the chat template a base model expects
options.B: Continue the text as a document would, perhaps with more quiz questions, rather than answer
options.C: Answer politely like a chat assistant, since question-and-answer text is all over its training data
options.D: Refuse, because a base model has no instructions telling it how to respond to users

options.A: Nothing much; scoring the prompt only costs a little more compute per training example
options.B: The model would forget its vocabulary, since prompt tokens would dominate every gradient step
options.C: Effort would go into predicting user messages, so the model learns to write prompts as well as answers
options.D: The causal mask would stop working, because the prompt tokens would then be able to see the answer after them

options.A: Smaller KV caches (shorter contexts, fewer KV heads), so more users fit in a batch
options.B: Larger decode batches, so each weight read is shared by more users
options.C: Longer contexts per request
options.D: Higher temperature
options.E: Quantized weights, so each tick reads fewer bytes

options.A: Only the weight values, via more training with the same next-token loss on curated prompt → answer pairs
options.B: The tokenizer is retrained for dialogue, so turns and roles get pieces of their own
options.C: A new answer-generation layer is added on top of the base model, and only that layer is trained on dialogue
options.D: The next-token loss is replaced by a reward score, so the model learns what people prefer

options.A: Training uses a KV cache to skip recomputation
options.B: Training needs several times the memory per parameter (gradients and optimizer state)
options.C: Serving updates the weights after every request
options.D: One failed GPU stalls a whole synchronized training job, so teams checkpoint often
options.E: Training GPUs must exchange gradients every step, so the network and stragglers matter as much as the chips

options.A: Adds a second, smaller model that tracks the conversation and hands the main model one turn at a time
options.B: Wraps each turn in special tokens like <|user|> and flattens the messages into one string to continue
options.C: Stores past conversations on the server so the model can recall them in a later session
options.D: Rewrites the user's prompt into a fixed question format, the one the base model saw most in pre-training

options.A: −ln p grows without limit as p → 0, so confident wrong answers are punished hard; 1 − p caps the penalty at 1
options.B: −ln p is cheaper to compute on a GPU than a subtraction across the whole vocabulary
options.C: There is no difference in what the model learns: both are lowest at p = 1, so −ln p is just convention
options.D: 1 − p can go negative when the model is very confident, which would reward a wrong answer instead of punishing it

options.A: A CDN edge cache: answers to common prompts are stored near users and served without running the model
options.B: Read replicas: each user in the batch gets a copy of the weights to read from in parallel
options.C: A circuit breaker: requests beyond the batch size are rejected until the GPU recovers
options.D: Group commit: many transactions share one disk flush, so each waits a bit longer but throughput rises
